blocks.text: Think Israel and a Palestinian state can coexist peacefully: U.S. Jews and Israeli Jews
A way can be found for Israel and an independent Palestinian state to coexist peacefully (% saying this).

Same Pew wording, different Pew surveys; each bar carries its own survey. Pew's Global Attitudes survey of spring 2014, a different survey from the 2014–15 Israel religion survey, gives 37% for Israeli Jews (https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2026/09/pg_2026.09.15_coexistence_report.pdf). No Pew figure for U.S. Jews on this question after 2020 was found.
Think Israel and a Palestinian state can coexist peacefully: all Israelis
A way can be found for Israel and an independent Palestinian state to coexist peacefully (% saying this), all Israeli adults.

In 2026, 56% of Israelis said it was not possible, the first time a majority said so (Pew). Includes Palestinian citizens of Israel, whom Pew labels "Israeli Arabs"; Pew notes many of them declined to answer in 2026.
Israeli Jews who place themselves on the right
Self-placement on a 1–7 left-right scale; 5–7 counted as right.

The Jewish People Policy Institute found 66% of Israeli Jews placing themselves on the right in July 2026, on a different scale; the two series should not be joined (https://www.timesofisrael.com/battle-for-the-center-large-majority-of-israelis-already-know-how-theyll-vote-poll/).
What Jewish Israelis say will decide their vote
The factor that will most influence which party they vote for, and the second most important factor (first and second choices combined).
IDI's own label for the last item is "judicial reform." Among Arab respondents (150), crime in Arab society led at 53.5%, then the economy at 46%.
Same question, two publics: U.S. "connected" Jews and Israeli Jews

Two JPPI survey rounds, each row dated. In the August 2025 rows the Israeli figures come from a separate JPPI survey, its Israeli Society Index, fielded earlier that month. JPPI's U.S. sample is a panel of "connected" Jews ("engaged" in the 2026 report), more engaged with Jewish life than U.S. Jews as a whole.
Israeli government policy contributes to antisemitism to a large extent
No connection between Israeli policy and antisemitism
Israel should not change its policy at all
Reports of famine in Gaza are true
Worried Israel is becoming a pariah

blocks.text: Trust in the Supreme Court: share answering "very much" or "quite a lot"

Selected years from IDI's annual series. Annual Democracy Index surveys, fieldwork usually in May; the 2025 survey is the latest (the 2026 index is expected in December). IDI's own label is "Arabs", and its Arab sample includes Druze; that sample is small (about ±5.1%) and swings widely from year to year. IDI also published a December 2023 reading from a different survey, the Israeli Voice Index; it is not part of this series and is not shown.
Trust in the Supreme Court among Jews, by group
Trust in the Supreme Court: share answering "very much" or "quite a lot", Jewish respondents

Annual Democracy Index surveys; the 2023 column is the June 2023 survey. Political camp is self-identified. The 2023 and 2024 camp figures are from the 2024 index (https://en.idi.org.il/media/27509/israel-democracy-index-2024-e_for_web_17-2-2025.pdf). December 2023 readings from the separate Israeli Voice Index are not shown. No 2026 breakdown by group has been published.
For and against the judicial overhaul, three IDI surveys
March 2026 wording: "Is it correct or not correct at this time to advance the judicial overhaul initiated by Justice Minister Yariv Levin?"
Three separate surveys with different questions; each row has its own source and date. Read them side by side, not as one trend line. The rest answered that they had no opinion or did not know.
January 2023: is the Levin plan good or bad?
January 2025: support or oppose the overhaul?

Share of valid votes in Daliyat al-Karmel, Yarka, Beit Jann, Hurfeish, Kisra-Sumei, Yanuh-Jat, Peki'in, Julis, Sajur and Ein al-Asad combined, computed from the Central Elections Committee's locality files. These are village results, not the vote of a group.

The leading lists of each election, ordered by their highest share; a dash means the list was not among the leading lists that year. Lists as they ran each year. Meretz ran within the Democratic Union in September 2019 (4.2%) and on a joint list with Labor–Gesher in March 2020. The Joint List parties and Ra'am row adds up the lists of Hadash, Ta'al, Balad and Ra'am as they ran each year: Hadash–Ta'al and Ra'am–Balad (April 2019), the Joint List (2019–2021), Ra'am (2021–2022), Hadash–Ta'al and Balad (2022). Counting Isfiya and leaving out Peki'in moves the 2022 shares by 1–2 points. Druze, Muslim and Christian respondents compared, 2025

IDI publishes these Druze, Muslim and Christian figures in its report (e.g. table 2.5) but says it "limited the use of" the religion breakdown "due to the small proportion of Christians and Druze in the Arab sample." The Druze subsample is about 31 people, so its margin of error is far wider than the full sample's

blocks.text: Economy and cost of living as a vote factor, by group

What will have the greatest influence on your decision regarding which party to vote for in the upcoming elections? Asked twice; the figure is the share naming "economy and the high cost of living" as the first or second factor.

Among all Jewish respondents, foreign affairs and security came first, at 39%; then economy 38%, conscription 27%, religion and state 26%, head of the party 23%. IDI did not publish the economy figure for Jewish respondents on the Right, where security leads at 47%. IDI's term is "Arab respondents" (its Arab sample). They ranked crime in Arab society first (53.5%); their option list replaced conscription with crime. Political camp is self-placement. No breakdown by religiosity was published. Before the 2022 election, 44% of all respondents named the economy and cost of living as their main factor (IDI, late July 2022, single choice, n=750), but the question and its options changed, with no conscription item, so the figures are not a series.
Share of each group in employment.

Rows come from different sources and periods; each row names its own. Haredi men's rate was 52% in 2015 and 53.1% in 2022; the government target is 65% by 2030. IDI also gives 53% for Haredi men in 2025. Taub's term is "Arab"; its summary does not say whether these figures include Druze. Taub gives no year for the non-Haredi Jewish men's figure.
Palestinian citizens of Israel, women (first half of 2025)
The war bill, as a share of GDP
Public debt, the government deficit and defense spending, each as a percentage of GDP.

Moody's 2026 figures are from its July 2026 summary (Ynet, https://www.ynetnews.com/business/article/rkqzvq4vfe); in February 2026 Moody's put debt at about 68% of GDP (Times of Israel), and the Bank of Israel's July forecast put 2026 debt at about 69% and the deficit at 4.9% (Jerusalem Post). Moody's deficit projection is for the central government. The 4.9% deficit ceiling is from the budget passed March 30, 2026 (Times of Israel, https://www.timesofisrael.com/knesset-approves-2026-budget-israels-largest-ever-sending-billions-to-haredi-institutions/). The Bank of Israel puts war-related costs for 2023–2026 at about NIS 350 billion.

People born in Ethiopia, and people born in Israel whose father was born in Ethiopia.

Each list's share of valid votes cast at Kiryat Malachi's ballot boxes.

blocks.text: The post-election clock in Basic Law: The Government
Time limits for forming a government after an election, as set in articles 7–13.
Different steps apply when a government falls mid-term (a no-confidence vote, art. 28, or a prime minister's dissolution order, art. 29).
The president, after consulting every list entering the Knesset
Within 7 days of the official results (art. 7)
The Knesset member given the task
28 days, plus up to 14 more at the president's discretion (art. 8)
The president picks another member, or tells the Speaker there is no prospect
Within 3 days; the second candidate has 28 days, no extension (art. 9)
A majority of Knesset members (61) may ask, in writing, for a named member
Request within 21 days; the president assigns the task within 2 days, and that member then has 14 days (art. 10)
Automatic if no request is made or the third attempt fails
New election on the last Tuesday before 90 days have passed (art. 11)
The Knesset, after the government presents its guidelines and ministers
A sitting within 7 days of the Knesset being notified (art. 13)

Each row cites its own Times of Israel report. Day counts are the days from election day to the swearing-in, computed from those dates. The December 2020 dissolution: IDI, Jan 28, 2026. Gantz's 2019 mandate: Times of Israel, Oct 23, 2019. The 2022 recommendations: Al Jazeera, Nov 11, 2022. Coalition parties: IDI, Apr 15, 2026. The 25th Knesset's dissolution: Ynet, July 17, 2026.
Netanyahu could not form a coalition in the 42 days allowed; the Knesset voted 74–45 to dissolve itself (May 30)
Netanyahu, then Gantz, failed; no candidate gathered 61 signatures in the 21-day window, and the Knesset dissolved (Dec 11)
Netanyahu–Gantz rotation government; the Knesset dissolved in December 2020 when the budget was not passed
May 17, 2020, by 73–46 (76 days after the vote)
Eight-party Bennett–Lapid government; the Knesset dissolved itself 92–0 on June 30, 2022
Netanyahu, recommended by 64 members, formed a six-party coalition; the Knesset served until July 2026
Knesset members in the coalition when each government was formed, 1992–2022
MKs in the coalition, as of the day the government was sworn in and up to a week afterwards.
Out of 120 seats. Elections in April and September 2019 produced no government, so they have no bar.

The most appropriate solution to drafting Haredim, November 2025

blocks.text: Who thinks a way can be found for Israel and an independent Palestinian state to coexist peacefully, 2013–2026

"Do you think a way can be found for Israel and an independent Palestinian state to coexist peacefully with each other?" Percent saying a way can be found. This asks whether coexistence is possible, not whether people want it.

Pew's label for the third column is "Arab Israelis". In 2026, 46% of Arab respondents gave no answer; 26% said a way cannot be found. Pew says the 2026 overall figure (17%) has not changed significantly from 2025 (21%). The 2014 figure for Jewish Israelis (37%) is from this Global Attitudes series; Pew's separate 2014–15 survey of religion in Israel, asking the same question, found 43% (see the note on the page).
Jewish Israelis who support each outcome, Peace Index, 2023–2026

"Regarding each of the following solutions to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, please state to what extent you support or oppose each of them." (March 2026 wording.) Percent of Jewish respondents who very much or moderately support.

Each option is rated separately, so the shares do not add up to 100. Sept 2023 values are read from the Peace Index chart; March 2026 values are rounded from 22.7, 37.7, 31.1 and 7.5. Sept 2023 report: https://en-social-sciences.tau.ac.il/sites/socsci-english.tau.ac.il/files/media_server/social/peaceindex/2023-09.pdf; Nov 2025 report: https://en-social-sciences.tau.ac.il/sites/socsci-english.tau.ac.il/files/media_server/social/peaceindex/2025-11.pdf

"Annexation of the occupied territories and the creation of one state under Israeli rule with limited rights for Palestinians"
"The creation of a binational state between the Jordan and the Mediterranean Sea with full and equal rights for Jews and Palestinians"

Support for "the creation of an independent Palestinian state alongside the State of Israel", among Jewish respondents who gave an opinion, by self-placement on the political spectrum.
Among opinion-holders only, so these figures are not comparable with the 23% of all Jewish respondents in the chart above.

blocks.text: Support for a civil marriage option, by group
"In general, do you support also having an option for civil marriage in Israel? (Civil marriage is marriage by the state rather than by religious authorities such as the Chief Rabbinate)"

Support is "strongly support" plus "somewhat support" in JPPI's table. Opposed: 60% of traditional-religious, 77% of religious and 85% of Haredi respondents. The last row is JPPI's "Arabs" (the source does not say whether Druze are included): 46% opposed and 15% did not know. All Israelis: 55% support.
Support for civil marriage when the question includes marriages between Jews and non-Jews
"What is your view on civil marriage if it would also include the possibility of marriages between Jews and non-Jews?"

A separate follow-up question in the same survey as the chart above, so the two charts are not one series. Support is "strongly support" plus "somewhat support" in JPPI's table. Opposed: 59% of traditional-not-religious, 87% of religious and 94% of Haredi respondents. The last row is JPPI's "Arabs": 48% opposed. All Israelis: 44% support, 50% opposed.
Support for public transport on Shabbat outside religious areas, Jewish respondents, by group
"Do you support or oppose operating public transportation on Saturdays (Shabbat) throughout the country, except in areas with major ultra-orthodox or religious populations?"

"Don't know" answers excluded. Left and right are respondents' own placement on a 1–7 scale. The report's text gives no April 2022 figure for the right; its lowest reading was 47.3% in September 2022. For all Jewish respondents (67.1% to 73.8%) and secular respondents (87.6% to 92.5%) it gives only the range across its surveys, not figures by date. The report gives no sample sizes.

documents.title: Chart labels: seats
documents.checked: Source dates are retained in the original chart data.

blocks.text: The share of valid votes a list needs to win any seats

IDI's Ofer Kenig gives the same steps (1% through 1988, 1.5% from 1992 to 2003, 2% for the next three elections) and dates the move to 3.25% to a law passed in March 2014, first applied in the 2015 election (IDI, January 26, 2015, https://en.idi.org.il/articles/5225). The two IDI articles agree once the year the law passed is separated from the year it was first used.
No legal threshold; one seat in 120 works out to 0.83%
Lists near the threshold in 2022, share of valid votes
Each list's votes as a share of 4,764,742 valid votes. The threshold was 154,855 votes; Meretz was 4,062 short and Balad 16,238 short.
Lists as they ran in 2022. In 2026 Hadash–Ta'al and Balad run together as the Joint List, and Labor and Meretz run together as The Democrats.
2022, step 3: whole seats at 36,227 votes each
Votes for the ten lists that passed the threshold, divided by 36,227 (4,347,342 ÷ 120), whole numbers only

The same seat price (36,227) and the same 113 whole seats appear in IDI's explainer (Ofer Kenig, March 16, 2026, https://en.idi.org.il/articles/63750). Religious Zionism–Otzma Yehudit was a joint list in 2022; in 2026 Religious Zionism runs with Zehut and Otzma Yehudit runs alone.
2022, step 4: the seven leftover seats, one round at a time
Each round, every list or surplus pair divides its votes by (seats it already has + 1); the highest result wins the next seat

Pairs with surplus agreements count as one list in this step. Labor (best figure 35,198.40) and Ra'am (32,341.17) never had the highest number. The same rounds, worked from the same totals, are in Matthew Shugart, Fruits and Votes, September 8, 2026 (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/2026/09/08/israels-bader-ofer-method-of-allocating-seats-step-by-step/).
Pairs of lists that agreed to count as one list when leftover seats are shared out

blocks.text: How many settlers: without and with East Jerusalem
Israeli Jewish residents of West Bank settlements.

Two sources, two definitions. Israel does not count East Jerusalem neighborhoods as settlements; the EU, the UN and Peace Now do. The registry compilation is published by Bet El Institutions, founded by former National Union MK Yaakov Katz; it is the only 2026 count found.
West Bank settlements, excluding East Jerusalem
Share of West Bank settlers in each group.

Two kinds of estimate. Yesha counts people by religiosity and does not say how. The other two rows give the share of settlers living in each type of settlement, not each person's own religiosity. IPF does not state its data year. The three agree only on the Haredi share, about a third.
Israel Policy Forum, 2025 (by type of settlement)
Modi'in Illit, in the West Bank, is not Modi'in, the city inside the Green Line.
How these towns voted in 2022, by type of settlement
Share of valid votes by locality group, 25th Knesset election. Turnout is a share of eligible voters.

How these towns voted, not how settlers voted. Settlements are CBS locality codes 3400–3899; East Jerusalem is inside Jerusalem's result and is excluded. Soldiers and others who vote by double envelope are counted nationally, not by home locality. The groups are this site's classification (see the list on the page).
How the settlements voted, 2019–2022, against Israel as a whole
Share of valid votes in all West Bank settlement localities, and in Israel as a whole.

How these towns voted. Each list is shown as it ran that year. The national-religious lists changed names and partners every cycle: URWP (2019) joined Jewish Home and Otzma Yehudit; Yamina was the alliance that included Naftali Bennett's New Right; in 2021 Religious Zionism ran Smotrich, Ben-Gvir and Noam together; in 2022 Religious Zionism and Otzma Yehudit ran as one list. Settlements are CBS locality codes 3400–3899, excluding East Jerusalem and double-envelope votes.
Settler attacks on Palestinians causing casualties or damage
Incidents in which settlers caused Palestinian casualties or property damage (UN OCHA count).

The IDF's own count of "nationalistic" Jewish incidents moves differently: 1,045 (2023), 682 (2024), 867 (2025), falling in 2024 where OCHA's count rose (JPost, Jan 19, 2026, https://www.jpost.com/israel-news/article-883857). The two bodies define incidents differently.

IDI's measure is turnout in "Arab and Druze localities": it includes Druze towns and leaves out Arab voters in mixed cities. blocks.text: Settlement housing units advanced in the West Bank, by year

Housing units in settlement plans advanced by the Higher Planning Council (deposit or validation), West Bank excluding East Jerusalem. Advanced means a plan cleared a planning stage, not that homes were built.

Each year comes from a separate Peace Now report. 2026 is a partial year: the same Peace Now page gave 8,056 units to July 29, 2026. In 2025 some plans passed both stages and are counted once. Counting East Jerusalem, the EU's 2025 settlements report puts 2025 at 63,311 units
Israelis' preferred approach to the Palestinians: separation, two states or annexation, June 2026
Preferred approach to the Israeli–Palestinian conflict (INSS's summary of the options).

All respondents. The remaining answers, about 13%, went to other options INSS did not list in its summary; among Arab respondents 21% chose one binational state. Jews: separation 32%, annexation without civil rights 31%. Arabs: two states 57%. Coalition voters: annexation 50%. Opposition voters: separation 40%, two states 36%
Full annexation without granting civil rights
Israelis who think Israel and a Palestinian state can coexist peacefully
"A way can be found for Israel and an independent Palestinian state to coexist peacefully." Share of all Israeli adults saying yes.

Same question each year; 2013–2025 are from Pew's June 2025 report, 2026 from its September 2026 report. Jews: 16% in both 2025 and 2026. Arab respondents: 40% in 2025 and 23% in 2026, but 46% of Arab respondents gave no answer in 2026, so the drop cannot be read as a change of mind. In 2026, 56% of all respondents said it was not possible
